title: The data on women at work call us to action
gist: World Bank data show women's labor force participation could take 350 years to match men's at the current pace; the global gap of about 30 points has barely moved since 1990. Country cases (Jordan, Indonesia, Azerbaijan, Turkiye) show targeted, data-driven policies can open jobs for women.

insights.claim: At the current pace of change, it could take 350 years for women to participate in the labor market at the same rate as men, based on trends in women's labor force participation from 1990 to today.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Structural gender gaps imply a persistent drag on global labor supply and growth.
insights.quote: At the current pace of change, it could take 350 years for women to participate in the labor market at the same rate as men.

insights.claim: Only about half of women aged 15 to 64 are engaged in income-generating work, around 30 percentage points below men, and that gap has barely changed since 1990.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Closing the gap represents a large untapped labor pool.
insights.locator: Longstanding gaps in women's economic participation

insights.claim: In several low-income countries, particularly in Sub-Saharan Africa, women's participation approaches 90 percent but is largely subsistence agriculture or informal trade without contracts or social protection, so high participation can reflect economic necessity rather than good jobs.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Participation rates alone are a poor indicator of job quality.
insights.locator: Global averages, however, tell only part of the story

insights.claim: In Jordan female labor force participation is among the world's lowest at around 15 percent, held back by social norms, mobility constraints and a formal economy not structured to absorb women, so needed measures differ from those in Tanzania or Rwanda.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Policy and investment must be tailored to country-specific barriers.
insights.locator: Contrast that with a country like Jordan

insights.claim: Jordan's Country Partnership Framework 2024-2029 targets raising female participation from roughly 14.8 percent to 28 percent by 2033 and ties private-sector job creation to safe childcare and public transport, supported by a US$221 million operation.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Childcare and transport investments are the identified binding constraints for Jordanian women.

insights.claim: By end-2025 in Jordan, close to 200 new nurseries were registered, close to 300 caregivers certified and over 1,600 working mothers received childcare subsidies.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Early implementation outputs for the childcare component are measurable.

insights.claim: World Bank analytics in 2024 modeled a potential $62 billion annual GDP gain in Indonesia if female labor force participation reaches 58 percent, feeding into a Care Economy Roadmap and parental leave legislation.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Care-economy investment is framed as a growth lever in Indonesia.
insights.locator: Indonesia illustrates the power of data

insights.claim: Azerbaijan opened 674 previously male-only occupations to women after finding blanket safety restrictions unjustified, replacing them with a health risk-based approach and improving its Women, Business and the Law score.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Removing legal job restrictions is a low-cost reform.

insights.claim: Türkiye's gains in women's employment over two decades came from structural shifts toward industry and services, falling fertility and rising education, and a World Bank-supported project pairing cooperatives with childcare and transport enabled over 500 women to access employment.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Structural transformation plus enabling services drive sustained female employment gains.
insights.locator: Türkiye offers perhaps the most instructive example

insights.claim: Gender data on earnings, job characteristics and working conditions in the informal economy, and on unpaid care work, remain deeply inadequate or collected inconsistently and infrequently.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Measurement gaps hide constraints and limit targeting; investment in gender data is called for.
insights.locator: Gender data as a development investment
